subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In which part of the Sun does nuclear fusion take place?
questions.explain: Fusion occurs in the extremely hot, dense core of the Sun.

questions.q: Dark lines seen in a star's spectrum (absorption lines) are useful because they reveal the star's:
questions.explain: Absorption lines are produced by elements in the star's atmosphere, so their pattern reveals what the star is made of.

questions.q: After leaving the main sequence, a Sun-like star first expands to become a:
questions.explain: As core hydrogen runs out, the star swells and cools into a red giant.

questions.q: Elements heavier than iron are mainly created during:
options: Quiet hydrogen burning on the main sequence
questions.explain: The extreme conditions of a supernova allow the formation of elements heavier than iron, which are then scattered into space.

questions.q: The visible 'surface' of the Sun that we see is called the:
questions.explain: The photosphere is the layer that emits the visible light we see as the Sun's surface.

questions.q: Absolute magnitude is defined as the brightness a star would have if it were placed at a standard distance of:
questions.explain: Absolute magnitude is the apparent magnitude a star would have at a standard distance of 10 parsecs, allowing true brightnesses to be compared.

questions.q: A very massive star is most likely to end its life in a:
options: Supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole
questions.explain: Massive stars explode as supernovae, leaving behind a neutron star or, for the most massive, a black hole.

questions.q: A star like the Sun will end its life as a:
questions.explain: After its red giant phase, a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf.

questions.q: The parallax method measures a star's distance by observing its:
options: Change in colour over a year
Apparent shift against background stars as the Earth orbits the Sun
questions.explain: Parallax uses the tiny apparent shift in a nearby star's position over six months to find its distance.

questions.q: The hottest stars, with surface temperatures above about 25,000 K, belong to which spectral class?
questions.explain: In the OBAFGKM sequence, O stars are the hottest and bluest, while M stars are the coolest and reddest.

questions.q: On a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram the axes plot luminosity against:
questions.explain: An H-R diagram plots luminosity (or absolute magnitude) against surface temperature, usually decreasing to the right.

questions.q: The region around a black hole from within which not even light can escape is bounded by the:
questions.explain: The event horizon is the boundary of a black hole beyond which the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.

questions.q: Apparent magnitude measures how bright a star:
options: Is compared with the Sun's mass
questions.explain: Apparent magnitude is the observed brightness from Earth; absolute magnitude is the true brightness.

questions.q: On the magnitude scale used for stars, a smaller (or more negative) number means the star is:
questions.explain: The magnitude scale runs backwards: brighter objects have smaller, even negative, magnitudes.

questions.q: A protostar becomes a true main-sequence star when:
options: It starts to shed its outer layers
Its core becomes hot and dense enough to begin nuclear fusion
It collapses into a black hole
questions.explain: Once the core reaches the temperature needed for hydrogen fusion, the protostar becomes a stable main-sequence star.

questions.q: On a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, most stars including the Sun lie on the:
questions.explain: The main sequence is the diagonal band where stars spend most of their lives fusing hydrogen.

questions.q: What stops a main-sequence star from collapsing under its own gravity?
options: The pressure from energy released by nuclear fusion in the core
questions.explain: The outward thermal pressure produced by core fusion balances the inward pull of gravity, keeping the star stable.

questions.q: What is the dense remnant left behind after a massive star explodes as a supernova, if it is not massive enough to form a black hole?
questions.explain: The collapsing core of a massive star can form an extremely dense neutron star after a supernova.

questions.q: The nearer a star is to us, the larger its measured:
questions.explain: Closer stars show a larger parallax shift, so distance in parsecs is the reciprocal of the parallax angle in arcseconds.

questions.q: Stars like the Sun produce their energy by:
options: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.explain: In the core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, releasing the enormous energy that powers a star.

questions.q: Which colour of star has the highest surface temperature?
questions.explain: Blue stars are the hottest, while red stars are the coolest.

questions.q: The stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun is the:
questions.explain: The solar wind is a continuous flow of charged particles released from the Sun's outer atmosphere.
